case_study_insert.main_stem: Earthwise Eco Blocks (EBM) is a private limited company in the eco-building-materials sector in south Wales, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Gareth Powell, it makes recycled composite building blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EBM plans to invest $760,000 in an automated eco-block moulding line using recycled quarry fines, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $228,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a block and a selling price of $10.00, and produces 90,000 units a year. EBM has two problems: waste from cracked blocks has risen and quality complaints from housebuilders reached 3.8% of deliveries last quarter.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q1 2026: The eco-block line moulded 21,600 blocks last quarter, of which 3.8% were cracked and rejected, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer complaints from housebuilders fell from 26 to 14 per month. Average cure time is 18 hours. Market research of 400 housebuilders found that 62% would pay up to $0.35 more for blocks containing recycled quarry fines, and 54% require environmental certificates on tender documents. A training audit shows 12 of 48 operatives have not used the new moulding line; certified off-the-job courses at the regional college cost $880 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Earthwise Eco Blocks for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, increasing debt-service costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills at labour-intensive moulding plants. (3) Wholesale prices of recycled quarry fines and cement have risen 9.8% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 5.6%, and the value of green-building tenders grew 4.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: EBM funded its $760,000 moulding line with a $400,000 bank loan and a $360,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for EBM of raising the $360,000 through a share issue rather than more bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike extra bank borrowing on top of EBM's $400,000 ten-year loan. With fixed costs of $228,000 a year and a $5.20 variable cost to cover on 90,000 units, avoiding further debt service protects cash flow and lets EBM spend on solving the 3.8% cracked-block rate instead of servicing lenders.

Point 2: equity holders share the risk of the $760,000 automated line, so if green-building demand disappoints there is no repossession threat to the moulding equipment and no damage to the credit record Gareth Powell may need later. A share issue also brings in investors with construction contacts, useful when 54% of surveyed housebuilders demand environmental certificates and EBM must win specifications. All $360,000 arrives at once, allowing the line to be commissioned before the next tender season rather than in stages dictated by loan drawdowns.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to EBM's financing mix and operating data.

questions.question_text: EBM wants builders to specify its recycled blocks in green-housing projects. Consider sponsoring a green-building trade exhibition, advertising in housebuilder trade magazines, or a social media campaign. Which should EBM choose to promote the new moulding line? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Green-building trade exhibition: An exhibition lets EBM show physical blocks and environmental certificates to specifiers face to face, and the 54% of 400 surveyed housebuilders who require such certificates can be given them immediately. Technical questions about recycled quarry fines can be answered on the spot, which helps justify a $0.35 premium. The drawback is high cost — stand fees and staff time are expensive for a firm funding a $760,000 line — and only a limited regional audience attends.

Housebuilder trade magazines: Advertising in specialist titles reaches the exact specification audience at lower cost than an exhibition and leaves a lasting record that procurement teams can file. It supports the tender-driven nature of the market. However, print is passive: readers may not respond quickly, and it cannot demonstrate block quality or answer concerns about the 3.8% cracked rate as effectively as a live demonstration.

Social media campaign: Posts showing the moulding line and recycled content can reach younger buyers cheaply with measurable engagement, and can reinforce the message that waste is falling from 5.1% to 3.8%. Yet housebuilders buy on tender and certification, not casual online interest, so conversion into the 21,600-block quarterly volume is uncertain.

Recommendation: EBM should sponsor the green-building trade exhibition. It uniquely combines demonstration, certification and personal contact with the specifiers who decide on green projects, making the $0.35 premium credible. Trade magazines are rejected as too passive to answer technical objections, and social media is rejected as unlikely to convert into the specification decisions that drive 90,000 units of output. EBM can follow up with low-cost magazine adverts after the exhibition.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to EBM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EBM with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of EBM with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: EBM still records a 3.8% cracked-block rate despite its flat structure and democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for EBM of introducing quality circles among its 48 operatives.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles let EBM's 48 operatives meet regularly to identify the causes of cracked blocks on the new moulding line, drawing on the practical knowledge of the 12 workers not yet trained on it. Because the flat structure already encourages participation, suggestions on mix moisture and cure time — currently 18 hours — can be tested quickly, reducing the 3.8% defect rate and the waste that raises the $5.20 variable cost per block.

Point 2: Involving operatives in solving complaints, which fell from 26 to 14 a month, raises ownership of quality and reduces the need for costly rework. Higher morale and commitment can lower labour turnover, saving the $880 per employee cost of certified courses, and supports the 62% of surveyed housebuilders who would pay $0.35 more for reliable recycled blocks. This protects the $10.00 selling price and the reputation needed to utilise the $760,000 line. With 21,600 blocks moulded last quarter and 18 hours of cure time, small process fixes suggested by operators can be tested quickly, so the benefit is practical as well as motivational.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EBM's defect rate, complaints, training costs and output.

questions.question_text: EBM must reduce cracked blocks on its new line. Consider end-of-line inspection or quality assurance built into the moulding process. Which should EBM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
End-of-line inspection: Checking finished blocks lets EBM catch the 3.8% that are cracked before they reach housebuilders, protecting the fall in complaints from 26 to 14 a month. It is simple to introduce and gives immediate feedback, and inspectors can record defects against the 21,600 blocks made last quarter. However, inspection detects rather than prevents faults: rejected blocks still consume materials and add to the $5.20 variable cost, and the 18-hour cure time means a bad batch is only found late, wasting capacity on the $760,000 line.

Quality assurance: Building checks into mixing, moulding and curing prevents cracks at source, which suits recycled quarry fines whose variation is a likely cause of the 3.8% rate. Working with quality circles in the flat structure, operators can adjust settings immediately, cutting waste and rework; with 62% of housebuilders willing to pay $0.35 more, consistent quality protects the premium. The drawbacks are the need to train the 12 untrained operatives (at $880 each if college courses are used) and a slower rollout while processes are redesigned.

Decision: EBM should choose quality assurance built into the moulding process. It attacks the cause of cracking rather than sorting out failures, which matters because waste is already raising unit costs on a 90,000-unit line. End-of-line inspection is rejected as a costly after-the-event filter that cannot recover the materials in rejected blocks; inspection can remain only as a final safety check once prevention is working. This also uses the flat structure and quality circles already present, so the 12 untrained operatives can learn from colleagues while defects are designed out, protecting the $0.35 premium and the 21,600-block quarterly output.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of inspection and assurance with limited application to EBM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of EBM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a well-justified decision covering prevention, cost and quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how EBM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $228,000 ÷ ($10.00 − $5.20) = $228,000 ÷ $4.80 = 47,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 47,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.00 − $5.20 = $4.80. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways EBM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 47,500-unit break-even output with 90,000 units produced to confirm a margin of safety of 42,500 units before the $760,000 moulding line becomes a risk.
2. Use the $4.80 contribution per unit to test the $0.35 premium: if all 90,000 blocks gained it, contribution would rise to $5.15, showing managers how much the 62% of interested housebuilders matter.
3. Set volume targets for the $400,000 bank loan: every block above 47,500 adds $4.80 toward interest and repayment, so monthly output of about 7,500 blocks covers fixed costs of $228,000.
4. Track unit cost ($228,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $5.20 = $7.73 a block) against the 3.8% cracked rate and the 9.8% rise in fines and cement prices in Appendix 3, so waste and inflation are spotted early.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 47,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.80 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 90,000 units; modelling the $0.35 premium on $4.80 contribution; loan-service targets on $228,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.73 to monitor cracks and inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EBM's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has EBM's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 1,440 ÷ revenue 3,600 × 100 = 40.0% in 2024; 1,848 ÷ 4,200 × 100 = 44.0% in 2025. Operating profit 432 ÷ revenue 3,600 × 100 = 12.0%; 630 ÷ 4,200 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit 432 ÷ capital employed 2,400 × 100 = 18.0%; 630 ÷ 2,800 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose from 3,600 to 4,200 while cost of sales increased from 2,160 to 2,352, so gross profit grew from 1,440 to 1,848. Capital employed rose from 2,400 to 2,800 as the $760,000 line was installed, and interest expense increased from 48 to 56.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably, so the improvement is consistent across trading and investment. The wider gap between revenue and cost of sales indicates better pricing or a better mix of recycled blocks, consistent with the 62% of housebuilders who would pay $0.35 more. Operating profit rose faster than revenue, showing overhead control despite higher interest. Returns on the larger asset base also improved, which is encouraging while the moulding line is new. A note of caution: the 3.8% cracked-block rate still wastes materials, and the 9.8% rise in fines and cement prices may compress the next year's figures unless the premium is secured.

Conclusion: EBM's profitability has improved. Gross and operating margins and returns on capital all increased together, so the conclusion is robust; management should lock in the $0.35 premium and cut cracking to protect the gain.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures with little or no accurate calculation of the three measures.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for EBM of making its blocks with recycled quarry fines instead of virgin aggregate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Research shows 62% of 400 housebuilders would pay up to $0.35 more for blocks containing recycled quarry fines, and 54% require environmental certificates. Using recycled fines therefore supports a premium that lifts contribution from $4.80 toward $5.15 per block and helps win specifications for green housing, protecting the 90,000-unit output needed for the $760,000 line. It also cuts waste from the 3.8% cracked rate being sent to landfill.

Disadvantage: Recycled fines can vary in composition, which may be a cause of the current 3.8% cracked-block rate and the 21,600-block quarterly reject count. If quality suffers, rework raises the $5.20 variable cost and the $0.35 premium may not be accepted, especially if the 5.6% construction-cost inflation makes builders price-sensitive. EBM may also need extra testing and certification to satisfy the 54% who demand environmental documents, adding cost before the new moulding line is fully productive. Managers must weigh the 62% interest against the 3.8% crack rate and the 54% certificate requirement before committing all 90,000 blocks to recycled fines.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EBM's research data, costs and defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in input costs will affect EBM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If EBM's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (derivation shown). This is small compared with fixed costs of $228,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates could still raise the cost of any further borrowing for the $760,000 line, though the 4.1% growth in green-building tenders supports demand.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, from $12.90 to $13.70 per hour): EBM has a workforce of 48 at a labour-intensive moulding plant, so the rise pushes up wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be calculated honestly; the right approach is qualitative, benchmarked against labour productivity of 90,000 units ÷ 48 workers = 1,875 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). If productivity slips while the 3.8% cracked rate persists, unit labour costs will rise and the $4.80 contribution from $10.00 less $5.20 will shrink.

Input cost inflation (9.8%): The insert does not break down the $5.20 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is derivable: if all of it rose 9.8%, that is 0.098 × $5.20 = $0.5096, about $0.51 a block; across 90,000 blocks this is 90,000 × $0.5096 = $45,864 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution materially, and with construction-cost inflation at 5.6% EBM may struggle to recover it, though the $0.35 premium accepted by 62% of housebuilders gives some cover.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 90,000 blocks and directly erodes the $4.80 contribution underpinning the $760,000 investment, whereas the interest change is a conditional $3,000 and the wage change cannot even be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. EBM should secure the premium and renegotiate recycled-fines supply contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to EBM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on EBM's costs or financing in context with shown arithmetic where figures are used.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context, with derivations shown and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
